The Longnose spurdog Squalus blainville is a relatively small, demersal squalid shark distributed across the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Neonates of this species emerge from their mothers at a total length of 16 centimeters [Lb = 16 centimeters], a size that reflects the constraints of uterine incubation in this viviparous shark. Pups are born following a gestation period that lasts approximately 518 days [ab = approximately 518 days] when the ambient water temperature is 17 °C [T = 17 °C], an extended developmental phase typical of many squaliform sharks. The prolonged gestation is linked to the energetic demands of yolk-dependent embryonic growth and the production of relatively large, well-developed young. At parturition, a newborn Longnose spurdog typically weighs around 50 grams [Wwb = around 50 grams], though reported values range from 45 to 55 grams, indicating some natural variation in maternal investment. This modest birth mass, combined with the substantial size at birth, suggests that neonatal pups are relatively advanced in their morphological development, allowing them to begin independent foraging shortly after emergence from the reproductive tract.

Reproduction in Squalus blainville follows a slow, K-selected life history strategy characteristic of many deep-water squalids. Females produce litters of 4 pups [N_R_i = 4 pups] following a biennial reproductive cycle in which 1 litter every two years [F_R_i = 1 litter every two years]. This leisurely reproductive tempo is maintained at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], which represents the typical thermal regime for this species across its geographic range. The low fecundity and long interval between successive litters result in a maximum intrinsic reproductive rate that is quite limited, consistent with the species' low natural mortality and extended lifespan. The energetic cost of producing even a small number of relatively large pups is substantial, and the two-year hiatus between litters likely allows females to fully replenish their energy reserves, accumulate sufficient yolk for the next batch of fertilised ova, and successfully complete the lengthy gestation period required for embryonic development.

The lifespan of the Longnose spurdog is remarkably extended for a shark of its body size. Individuals have been documented to reach a maximum longevity of 5475 days [am = 5475 days] when living under the thermal conditions characteristic of their habitat, specifically a sustained water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This long lifespan, exceeding fifteen years, is a classic correlate of the species' delayed maturation, low fecundity, and slow metabolic pace. The combination of late maturity and extended reproductive lifespan allows females only a limited number of reproductive events over their lifetime, given the two-year interval between litters. This life history constellation renders the Longnose spurdog particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as populations cannot recover quickly from even modest increases in adult mortality. The maximum recorded longevity of 5475 days underscores the necessity of careful, precautionary management for this slow-growing squalid.

Sexual maturation in the Longnose spurdog is highly dimorphic in terms of timing. Under the typical thermal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], female sharks attain puberty approximately 1862 days after birth [tp = approximately 1862 days after birth], a delay of more than five years that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to reach the body size necessary for successful gestation. In contrast, males reach sexual maturity much earlier, with puberty occurring about 1205 days after birth [tp = about 1205 days after birth] under these identical conditions, a pronounced difference in maturation timing that is common among elasmobranchs and generally attributed to the contrasting energetic demands of male versus female reproductive at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] roles. Males, which do not bear the burden of gestation, can allocate resources toward growth and gonad development at a faster rate, reaching reproductive competence several years before their female counterparts.

Comparative studies among members of the genus Squalus highlight the conservative life history of Squalus blainville relative to its congeners. The age at birth of approximately 518 days [ab = approximately 518 days] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is a relatively protracted gestation period, exceeding that reported for some smaller squalid species, such as Squalus acanthias, and likely reflects the energetic demands imposed by producing relatively large pups under the stable thermal conditions of the temperate continental shelf. Following parturition, juveniles enter a prolonged sub-adult phase during which they forage on small teleosts and cephalopods, gradually building the body mass necessary for eventual reproduction, a drawn-out developmental trajectory that empirically substantiates the life-history trade-off between slow growth and extended longevity characteristic of this deep-water elasmobranch.
